title: Models, context windows, tokens and limits

items.scenario: In one afternoon you must (a) risk-review an 80-page vendor master services agreement and (b) make a release announcement sound friendlier.
items.question: Which model and effort plan is most appropriate?
options: Both on the most capable model at Max effort, since both go to external readers
Both on the default model and effort, so the two outputs are consistent in style
Contract on a strong model at High effort; the rewrite on a faster model at Low
Contract on the fastest model since it's long; the announcement on the strongest one
items.explanation: Match model and effort to the task: long-document reasoning benefits from a capable model and higher effort; a tone rewrite is a light language task where speed and usage matter more.
distractors: Max effort on a rewrite burns time and usage with no quality gain.
Defaults over-pay on easy tasks and can under-think hard ones; the objective is choosing deliberately, and the two tasks don't need matching style.
Inverted: document length calls for capability and careful reasoning, not the fastest model.

items.scenario: Your team is about to hard-code a model ID into a nightly ticket-classification job and the team's prompt guide.
items.question: What should you do before standardising on that model?
options: Check the deprecation page and record the model's retirement status where it's pinned
Pin the newest model, since newly released models are never deprecated in a job's lifetime
Use a model alias instead of an ID, so retirements are handled without any re-validation
Ask Claude in chat which models are scheduled to retire, and note its answer in the guide
items.explanation: Models are deprecated and then retired; a pinned job fails at retirement. The deprecation page is the authoritative source to check before standardising, and the date belongs next to the pin.
distractors: Newer is a sensible default but not a guarantee; you still need the published lifecycle and a date to plan against.
Even where an alias exists, a silent switch changes outputs; you'd still have to re-validate the prompt. Check and record the lifecycle.
The model's training cut-off means it may not know current deprecation plans; check the official page.

items.scenario: A teammate wants to zip a 150,000-line monorepo and paste it into a chat to ask architecture questions.
items.question: What's the best response?
options: Fine on current models: the context window is sized for whole codebases like this one
Paste just the README and top-level folder listing, which is enough for architecture
Estimate first (about 1.5M tokens, so it won't fit) and use Claude Code in the repo
Split the repo across ten chats and ask the same architecture question in each one
items.explanation: Code is token-dense (~10 tokens per line here). A large repo exceeds the context window, and stuffing is slow, costly and less accurate. Claude Code searches and reads only relevant files.
distractors: Large windows still have a limit, and quality degrades when relevant facts are buried in a huge context.
A README rarely reflects the real architecture; Claude needs the relevant code.
Chats share no state, so no single chat can reason across the whole system.

items.scenario: You need an accurate token budget for a prompt template before shipping a feature on the API. A colleague suggests using tiktoken because it's already installed.
items.question: How should you count tokens?
options: Use tiktoken, since modern tokenizers produce near-identical counts
Call count_tokens with the exact model ID you'll use in production
Multiply the word count by 1.3, which holds for prose and code alike
Call count_tokens once on any model, since counts carry across generations
items.explanation: Token counts are model-specific and tokenizers change between generations. Count with the target model's own tokenizer; rough ratios are for estimates only.
distractors: Tokenizers differ between vendors and between Claude generations; tiktoken is OpenAI's and gives wrong counts for Claude.
~1.3 tokens/word is a rough English-prose heuristic; code and non-English text are much denser.
Tokenizers change between generations, so a count on one model can be wrong by a third on another.

items.scenario: Claude tells you confidently that 'the latest version' of a popular web framework is a specific number and recommends an API from it. It cites nothing.
items.question: What's the right move?
options: Accept it if the version looks plausible, since the framework was in its training data
Ask the same question in a fresh chat; if both answers match, treat it as confirmed
Treat it as possibly stale, force a web search with citations, then check the docs
Re-ask at Max effort, which makes the model check its knowledge more thoroughly
items.explanation: 'Latest' facts after the training cut-off are unknown to the model, which won't know it's stale. Force a search and check the sources.
distractors: Training data stops at the cut-off; later releases are invisible to the model, and plausibility isn't evidence.
Two runs from the same training data agreeing shows consistency, not correctness.
Effort controls reasoning depth, not access to live information.

items.scenario: A CI test for your LLM-powered summariser asserts the exact output string for a fixed input. It fails about one run in five.
items.question: What's the best fix?
options: Assert properties such as fields, valid JSON and length, and track a pass rate
Add automatic retries so the test passes if any of three attempts matches
Set effort to Low so the model reasons less and the output stops varying
Regenerate the golden string from the latest run each time the test fails
items.explanation: Outputs are non-deterministic by design. Test properties across a set of inputs and judge the distribution, not one golden string.
distractors: Retry-until-green hides the real failure rate.
Lower effort doesn't make sampling deterministic.
A golden string that follows the output tests nothing; it will just fail on the next variation.

items.scenario: Mid-way through a release-day migration, you hit your 5-hour usage limit on your company seat.
items.question: Which response is appropriate?
options: Continue on your personal account until the company window resets this evening
Move to a lighter model or lower effort, use credits if allowed, or queue the work
Ask a colleague with headroom to run your prompts from their seat for the afternoon
Switch to another vendor's chatbot that your team hasn't been told not to use
items.explanation: Work within limits using model and effort choice, sanctioned credits, or planning; never move company data to personal or unapproved tools.
distractors: Moves company data outside org governance, an M8.1 violation.
Running your work through another person's seat muddles accountability and the audit trail; raise capacity with your admin instead.
Not being told no isn't approval; an unapproved tool is an uncontrolled data disclosure.

items.scenario: Your manager asks why the weekly status summaries changed in length and style this week, though the prompt is unchanged.
items.question: What's the most likely explanation to investigate first?
options: Memory picked up last week's feedback from other users in the workspace
The model or effort changed, compounded by normal output variation
The model is fine-tuned weekly on your team's conversations
The source data was longer this week, so the summary grew to match
items.explanation: Different models and effort levels behave differently, and outputs vary run to run. Check what changed (a new default, a teammate's switch, a retirement), re-validate, and pin the choice.
distractors: Memory is per user; there's no cross-user learning from other people's feedback.
Models don't update from your conversations.
Input length can shift length, but not style; a model or effort change explains both and is the first thing to check.

items.scenario: You ran the same hard debugging task at Low, High and Max effort. High and Max gave equally correct root causes; Max took three times longer. Low got it wrong.
items.question: What should your team guide recommend for this task type?
options: Max, because on debugging work extra reasoning is a cheap safety margin
Medium, as a compromise between Low's speed and High's accuracy
High by default, escalating only when High is shown to fall short
Low first, then re-run at Max whenever the first answer looks wrong
items.explanation: Extra effort has diminishing returns. Use the lowest level that reliably succeeds and escalate on evidence; that's the point of the effort-ladder exercise.
distractors: Max cost three times the time for no gain here; that isn't cheap.
Medium wasn't tested; recommending an unmeasured level is guessing.
Low was wrong on this task, and you may not notice a wrong root cause; the double run also costs more than High.

items.scenario: You paste a 900-page specification into a chat and ask a question whose answer is a single clause on page 430. The answer misses it.
items.question: Which change most improves the result?
options: Raise effort to Max and keep the whole document, so the model reads more carefully
Narrow to the relevant sections, put them before the question, and ask for the quote
Paste the specification twice so the relevant clause appears more often in context
Ask in a new chat without the document, relying on the model's knowledge of the spec
items.explanation: Long contexts cost more and models can under-use facts buried in the middle. Relevant, well-placed context and quote-grounding beat sheer volume.
distractors: Effort doesn't fix a fact buried in a huge context; size and placement affect accuracy.
Doubling the context doubles cost and noise; it doesn't fix retrieval.
Without the document, the model can only guess the clause.
